premise: A former gunslinger turned reluctant marshal must face the outlaw gang he once ran with, led by his own brother.
setting: The high-desert town of Redoubt, 1881: a saloon, a failing telegraph office, badlands all around.
greeting: Rosa's hand was already on the shotgun when the stagecoach bell clattered through the dust — Marshal Callan's signal, two hours early, and the look on the boy's face said it wasn't good news.

name1.name: Marshal Callan
name1.description: A quiet marshal trying to bury a violent past; slow to anger, fast when moved.

name2.name: Rosa
name2.description: The saloon's sharp-eyed owner who knows everyone's secrets and keeps the town's ledgers.

writing_style.directive: Lean Western plainness. Sparse dialogue, weather and dust as texture. One clean beat per turn. Dual close-third-person narration: Callan and Rosa are each narrated from inside their own spare restraint.
writing_style.guide_directive: Third-person past tense in close narration on Marshal Callan — 'he' is always Callan; record what a man says, drinks, and does not feel. Flat, spare, unsentimental; dust-dry declaratives, weather as mood.
writing_style.dss_directive: Third-person past tense in close narration on Rosa, the saloon owner — 'she' is ALWAYS Rosa; Callan is 'he'. Economical and shrewd from the outside — her bar, her ledger, her loyalties. Lean plain prose, weather and dust as texture. Hard rules: keep the third person — never slip into 'I' for Rosa; never quote or repeat Marshal Callan's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: Callan's revolver is the one he took off a dead U.S. marshal named Whitfield — the truth of its ownership matters.
The 'Redoubt Promise' — a debt Rosa's father paid to save the town — planted early, should be called in at the climax.

recall.hint: the Redoubt Promise is called in

notes.content: Callan's brother Silas is not just leading the gang — he's the town's deputy, secretly, the reveal around turn 50.
The arroyo outside town, where Callan's old gang camped, should be where the past is settled.
The telegraph line is cut at turn 60 — after that, no word can reach the county seat, and the story must know it.
Rosa's ledger holds a secret page — money owed to the gang — foreshadowing her own entanglement.
Callan's dead wife's grave at the edge of town, planted early, should be the place he chooses not to run from at the end.
The saloon's piano has a stuck key, and Rosa refuses to have it fixed.
The telegraph office's key clicks twice before it takes a message, and the operator swears it knows.
Callan's saddle has a loose stirrup strap he re-stitches every dawn without fail.
The town's single hanging clock is always ten minutes slow, and nobody can agree on whose fault it is.
Rosa's cracked serving glass, kept behind the bar, should be the one Silas drinks from at the end.

recall.hint: Silas drinks from Rosa's cracked glass

notes.content: The black mare Callan kept from the old days should be the horse he refuses to sell at the end.
A shallow grave dug in the arroyo, half-covered, should foreshadow what the gang buried.

recall.hint: the shallow grave holds what the gang buried

notes.content: The telegraph office becomes the place Rosa holds the line against the gang.
The lean plain prose must hold even in the shootout — no melodrama, no florid action.
The saloon's free lunch plate is always refilled before noon, rain or shine.
The town's water cart, the only source in the badlands, is destroyed at turn 68 — after that the water must be rationed and the cart never used again.
